summary: Fort Point Light, on the headland at the mouth of Trinity Harbour, Newfoundland, first lit in 1874; the Rowe family kept it for 88 years and sources report it still staffed.

structures.note: Painted white; the 1874 notice puts the light at 75 feet above sea level. The 3D gallery gives the first tower as 23 m above sea level.
About half the height of the wooden tower. The gambrel-roofed building under the wooden tower was kept and joined to the iron tower by a covered passageway.
On lower ground south of the lighthouse; diaphone fog alarm.
Erected after the iron tower was demolished on 25 June 1971.

The Coast Guard list gives 'Square skeleton tower' and 12.4 m. Lighthouse Friends dates it to about 2003. The 3D gallery calls it a wooden structure of 2003. The Coast Guard list names no material; the 3D gallery says wooden.

staffing.basis: Lighthouse Friends says the second keeper's building is still occupied by the Coast Guard; the DFO brochure (page modified 2019-09-24; copyright 2005) lists Fort Point among staffed lightstations.

access.note: Coast Guard property and a staffed lightstation. Lighthouse Friends says the grounds are open and the tower closed.

events.note: Work began in 1872; a notice announced the completion of the lighthouse in 1873.
Fixed white light from 1 January 1874, per the mariners' notice.
Eighth-order dioptric apparatus with a single argand burner, arc of 320 degrees.
Lens damaged when a lamp glass chimney exploded, per Inspector Nevill's 1877 report as quoted by Lighthouse Friends.
Fixed white changed to occulting white, 6.25 s light and 1.25 s dark.
Fog alarm building added south of the lighthouse; diaphone sounded by air compressed by oil engines.
Wooden tower replaced by a circular iron tower about half as tall.
Schooner Marion Rogers ran aground a few metres from the fog alarm building on 27 November 1938; seven men lost.
Keeper Henry James Rowe retired at 65, ending 88 unbroken years of lightkeeping by the Rowe family.
Iron tower demolished on 25 June 1971; red skeleton tower 4.3 m erected.
Present tower built around 2003 (Lighthouse Friends) and 2003 (3D gallery).
Trinity Historical Society announced plans to convert one of the two keepers' homes into an interpretation centre.

corrections.why: Lighthouse Friends says the lighthouse is owned by the Canadian Coast Guard. The Trinity Historical Society runs the historic site, not the light. The record's value is also cut off mid-name.
The lighthouse is owned by the Canadian Coast Guard (Lighthouse Friends), a federal agency. The nonprofit is the historic-site society.

resolved_conflicts.explanation: The record's 2003 date for the present tower is supported by Lighthouse Friends (around 2003) and the 3D gallery (2003). The Coast Guard list gives a square skeleton tower and no material, so it does not contradict the 3D gallery's wooden structure.

notes_for_editor: Sources disagree and the story states the disagreements: (1) First battery: Lighthouse Friends says 1744; the Trinity Historical Society says the fort was fortified in 1746. (2) Present tower material: Coast Guard list 'Square skeleton tower', 12.4 m; 3D gallery 'wooden structure' of 2003; Lighthouse Friends 'around 2003' without material. (3) Visibility of the first light: the 1874 notice says eleven miles; the 3D gallery gives 9.5 nautical miles. (4) Passengers on the Marion Rogers: Lighthouse Friends gives six crew and one passenger; the Advocate names Butler and McGrath as passengers among its seven men. (5) Position in the 1874 notice: Lighthouse Friends gives 48 21 55 N, 53 26 54 W; the Coast Guard list gives 48 21 55.9 N, 053 20 45.2 W. The longitudes differ by about 6 arc-minutes (about 7.6 km). The notice may have a transcription error. Not resolved; not in the story. Other points: The Advocate's crew list spells the name McGarth; the story uses McGrath from the passenger line. The Advocate article is read through a transcription, not a scan. The 1938 inquiry and the 1877 to 1889 inspector quotations are read only as Lighthouse Friends quotes them; the originals were not read. Keepers: two William Rowes are listed, the 1906 to 1910 one not linked; Arch. Rowe not linked to William Arthur Rowe. Thomas Pike and W. Connolly are listed under Fog Alarm and recorded as 'other'. Fog signal: the record says horn; the Coast Guard list gives 'Fog Horn' with 'Blast 2 s; sil. 18 s' (now in the story, under Today); the 1910 diaphone was a separate signal. The lens of 1874 and any current lens are not described in any source read. Staffing: the story attributes 'still a staffed station' to Lighthouse Friends and the DFO brochure (page modified 2019-09-24; copyright 2005), so the brochure's staffed list may be older than its page date; the record's check flag is not cleared by these sources alone, so a human should confirm before saying it is staffed today. The Trinity Historical Society hours page is undated. Do not confuse with Fort Point at LaHave, Nova Scotia (Fort Point Museum), which is a different place. Not verified on the ground. Revised 2026-10-28 by the fact-checker: the Advocate's doubt about the schooner's destination and the 3D gallery's 9.5 nautical mile range are now stated in the story; the story no longer calls the 1938 night 'most remembered' or describes two sources as disagreeing on material; five sentences missing footnotes were footnoted; units now read 23 m (75 ft).
